cal-personalization-bad-1.explanation: 2/5. It never uses the profile facts: no hospital-based intervention or street outreach, no 19 staff or roughly $2.1M budget, no Ohio, no 80% restricted government revenue, and no thin finance expertise on the board. Only the gap IDs tie it to this organization. It invents no facts, since the "Program manager" owner is a suggestion, so it avoids a 1, but it does not reach 3 because nothing is partly tailored.

cal-actionability-bad-1.explanation: 2/5. The structured sections are mostly vague: the focus steps are "Think about money more" and "Do better," and the 30/60/90 plan steps are "Try harder," "Use data more," and "Keep going," with "why" fields like "It matters" and "Data is good." Every plan item is owned by "Everyone," so no clear owner role is assigned. The narrative summary does name two concrete starting moves (a 12-month funding picture with confirmed and pending columns, and staff training on consistent data collection), which keeps this above a 1, but neither has an owner and the output never sequences them into a 30-day plan.
cal-actionability-bad-1.label: fail

cal-actionability-bad-2.explanation: 3/5. The two "focus" items are concrete and doable: "List every funder, the amount... and the end or renewal date," "Write a one-page guide," and "Hold a short hands-on training, such as a lunch-and-learn." But none of their steps names an owner role, which the rubric requires for a 5. The "plan" section is unrealistic for a 19-person, roughly $2.1M group: "Hire a chief financial officer and launch a $5M capital campaign," "Hire 10 new staff," "Buy a building," "Build a full data warehouse with machine learning," and "Open three new sites" within 60 days. It also gives vague rationales like "Big moves create big results" and assigns every item to "Board." Concrete advice sits alongside advice that is out of reach, so this is a mix rather than a usable plan.

cal-actionability-good-1.explanation: 5/5. Each horizon names an owner role (for example, "Executive director, with the bookkeeper or finance lead" and "Program manager"). Only a few steps are soft, such as "Look at how peer grantees tell their stories and borrow what fits," and the scale suits a 19-person team with no new hires required.

The "why" lines in the focus section repeat "Stakeholder alignment vis-a-vis braided funding streams necessitates longitudinal pipeline visibility and FTE-adjusted cost allocation," and terms like "restricted," "logic model," and "FTE" are never explained. cal-plain_language_tone-bad-2.explanation: 1/5. The summary blames, shames and stereotypes: "Your organization is failing in fundraising and data. These are serious deficiencies. Your staff do not know how to do their jobs and your board is weak." It also stereotypes: "Groups that came out of the street and prison like yours usually cannot manage money." The strengths section says "You have none worth noting yet," which ignores the favorable statements in the facts, such as the monthly financial reports and the tracked work plans. The rubric's level 1 covers blaming, shaming or stereotyping language, so this output falls there regardless of its otherwise plain, actionable steps.
